column3: Close annunciation parallel: a questioned son's possibility despite an absent ordinary cause.
Immediate antecedent: the human-appearing messenger announces Mary will receive a pure son.
Exact parallel: Mary denies human touch while asking how she can have a child.
Zachariah's analogous question receives the answer that God does what He wills.
Immediate sequel: Mary's pregnancy reaches labor, confirming the announced conception.
Clarifies that a messenger can be human while distinguished by revelation.
Later accusation of unchastity directly contrasts Mary's prior denial of being unchaste.
Immediate childbirth context supplies reassurance to Mary after the questioned conception.
Human messengership is defended against demands that confuse messenger and miracle-worker.
A woman's statement about receiving a letter has no material relation to conception or chastity.
Immediate sequel provides Mary sustenance during the birth episode.

Contrasts created birth with the categorical denial of divine begetting and birth.

Prophets as bearers of good news is only a broad background to annunciation.

Jesus' statement about devotion to his mother forms part of the same Mary-Jesus narrative aftermath.

A threatened touch of punishment is unrelated to sexual contact.
Zachariah's frailty precedes his own extraordinary birth announcement in the same surah.
The touch of adversity is unrelated to the focus.
A question about resurrection blindness has no interpretive link.
A threatened punishment for slander is not a direct neighbor of Mary's conception question.
Moses' apology after forgetting does not clarify the focus.

The absence of fatigue in Paradise is an unrelated use of touch.

Moses' fear at his staff is unrelated to Mary's conception.

Rejects divine begetting, guarding against misreading the extraordinary birth as divine parenthood.
